title: Organic Chemistry for Health Sciences
description: Reaction mechanisms, stereochemistry, and the chemistry of alcohols, carbonyl compounds, acids, amines and aromatic compounds relevant to drugs and biomolecules.

topics.title: Reaction Mechanisms
topics.summary: Bond cleavage, nucleophiles and electrophiles, and substitution, addition and elimination reactions.

notes.b: Covalent bonds break by homolysis (each atom takes one electron, forming free radicals — e.g. in chlorination of alkanes under UV light) or heterolysis (one atom takes both electrons, forming ions — carbocations and carbanions). Nucleophiles are electron-rich species that donate an electron pair (OH−, CN−, NH3, H2O); electrophiles are electron-poor and accept an electron pair (H+, carbocations, NO2+). Carbocation stability increases from methyl < primary < secondary < tertiary because of inductive and hyperconjugation effects.
k: Nucleophile donates, electrophile accepts electron pairs

notes.b: SN2 reactions are single-step, bimolecular, favoured at primary carbons, and cause inversion of configuration (Walden inversion). SN1 reactions are two-step via a carbocation, favoured at tertiary carbons, and give racemisation. Elimination (E1, E2) forms alkenes, favoured by strong bulky bases and heat; Zaitsev's rule predicts the more substituted alkene. Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition; Markovnikov's rule states that H adds to the carbon already bearing more hydrogens. Aromatic rings undergo electrophilic substitution (nitration, halogenation, Friedel–Crafts).
k: SN2: one step, inversion, primary carbons
Markovnikov: H to the carbon with more H

topics.title: Stereochemistry and Drug Action
topics.summary: Chirality, enantiomers, R/S nomenclature, geometric isomerism and their pharmaceutical importance.

notes.b: A chiral molecule is non-superimposable on its mirror image, usually because of a carbon bearing four different groups (a stereocentre). The two mirror-image forms are enantiomers: they have identical physical properties except the direction in which they rotate plane-polarised light (dextrorotatory + / laevorotatory −). A 50:50 mixture is a racemic mixture (optically inactive). Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images and have different physical properties. Meso compounds have stereocentres but an internal plane of symmetry, so they are achiral. Absolute configuration is assigned R or S using Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priority rules.
k: Enantiomers rotate light in opposite directions

notes.b: Receptors and enzymes are chiral, so enantiomers can differ in potency or toxicity. The (R)-enantiomer of thalidomide is sedative while (S)-thalidomide is teratogenic (and they interconvert in the body). S-(−)-propranolol is the active β-blocker; escitalopram is the active S-enantiomer of citalopram; levodopa (L-DOPA) is used in Parkinson's disease rather than D-DOPA. Geometric (cis–trans / E–Z) isomers arise around double bonds or rings; e.g. cisplatin is active while transplatin is not.
k: Escitalopram and levodopa are single enantiomers

topics.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
topics.summary: Classification, properties and reactions of alcohols, phenols and ethers.

notes.b: Alcohols (R–OH) are primary, secondary or tertiary depending on the number of carbons attached to the carbinol carbon. Hydrogen bonding gives them higher boiling points than alkanes of similar mass. Oxidation: primary alcohols → aldehydes → carboxylic acids; secondary → ketones; tertiary resist oxidation (the basis of the dichromate breathalyser and Lucas test differences). Ethanol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetaldehyde, then to acetic acid; methanol is metabolised to formaldehyde and formic acid, causing blindness and acidosis (treated with fomepizole or ethanol).

Phenols have –OH attached directly to a benzene ring; they are more acidic than alcohols because the phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised, and they give a violet colour with neutral ferric chloride. Phenol (carbolic acid) was Lister's antiseptic; derivatives include cresols and chloroxylenol (Dettol). Ethers (R–O–R′) are relatively unreactive; diethyl ether was an early general anaesthetic, and modern volatile anaesthetics (isoflurane, sevoflurane) are halogenated ethers.
k: Phenols are more acidic than alcohols

topics.title: Aldehydes, Ketones, Carboxylic Acids and Esters
topics.summary: Carbonyl chemistry, identification tests, acids, esters and their hydrolysis.

notes.b: The carbonyl group (C=O) is polar; its carbon is electrophilic and undergoes nucleophilic addition. Aldehydes are readily oxidised, so they reduce Tollens' reagent (silver mirror) and Fehling's/Benedict's solution (brick-red Cu2O); ketones generally do not. 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (Brady's reagent) gives orange precipitates with both. Methyl ketones and ethanol give yellow iodoform with iodine and alkali. Formaldehyde solution (formalin) is a tissue fixative; acetone is a solvent and ketone body.
k: Iodoform test: methyl ketones and ethanol

notes.b: Carboxylic acids (–COOH) are weak acids, stronger when electron-withdrawing groups are nearby (trichloroacetic acid > acetic acid). They react with alcohols in acid to form esters (esterification, reversible). Esters hydrolyse in acid or base (saponification with NaOH makes soap from fats). Many drugs are esters (aspirin — acetylsalicylic acid, benzocaine) or amides (paracetamol, lidocaine); esters are generally hydrolysed faster than amides, so ester local anaesthetics have shorter action. Aspirin tablets that smell of vinegar have hydrolysed to salicylic and acetic acid.

topics.title: Amines, Amides and Heterocycles in Drugs
topics.summary: Basicity of amines, amide bonds, and important heterocyclic rings in medicines and biomolecules.

notes.b: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia: primary (RNH2), secondary (R2NH), tertiary (R3N) and quaternary ammonium salts (R4N+, permanently charged, e.g. neuromuscular blockers, which cannot cross the blood–brain barrier). Amines are basic because of the lone pair on nitrogen; aliphatic amines are more basic than aromatic amines like aniline (whose lone pair is delocalised into the ring). Most drugs that are weak bases form water-soluble salts (e.g. hydrochlorides). Amides (–CONH2) are very weakly basic because the lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen; the peptide bond is an amide bond.
k: Aliphatic amines are more basic than aniline

notes.b: Heterocyclic rings contain atoms other than carbon (N, O, S). Important examples: pyridine (nicotinamide/NAD+), pyrimidine (cytosine, thymine, uracil; also in trimethoprim), purine (adenine, guanine, caffeine), imidazole (histidine; azole antifungals such as clotrimazole), indole (tryptophan, serotonin), quinoline (quinine, chloroquine), thiazole (thiamine) and the β-lactam ring (penicillins, cephalosporins). The β-lactam ring's strain explains both its antibacterial activity and its susceptibility to β-lactamases.

q: Which compound is the strongest base?
Aliphatic amines are more basic than aromatic amines and amides.
